```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                     fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.25)
```

A model covariate can be a kernel-weighted mean, a surface texture, or a
categorical landscape metric. That definition must survive preparation,
fitting, prediction, plotting, and model comparison. This guide follows those
steps and identifies the inference methods that support each feature.

Start with `vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` for the basic
workflow. The artificial landscape below demonstrates software behavior. Its
counts do not provide evidence of scale recovery, ecological effects, or
interval coverage. Optimization and posterior fitting examples are not run
during the vignette build.

## Choose features and a fitting method

`kernel_var()` estimates the distance scale of an environmental mean.
`surface_var()` describes variation in a continuous surface, while
`landscape_var()` describes categorical composition or configuration. An
unweighted metric uses a circular neighborhood with a hard boundary. Its radius
can be fixed or estimated. A weighted surface metric uses the selected kernel
and estimates its bandwidth instead. With `kernel = "fixed"`, that parameter
is a hard cutoff radius for kernel means and weighted metrics alike. Their
metric formulas and training normalization are retained. Radius SEs and
Wald limits are missing; request `summary(fit, profile = TRUE)` for profile
limits and inspect the stepped likelihood. Native coefficient SEs remain
conditional on the selected radius. Fitted distance tables and kernel
plots show the full radius in both dimensional definitions.

| Feature | Native refit | Analytic likelihood backends | Bayesian scales |
|:--------|:-------------|:----------------------------|:----------------|
| Kernel mean | Gaussian, exponential, exponential-power, or fixed kernel | Supported smooth kernels under the chosen backend's contract | Gaussian or exponential |
| Weighted surface SQ | Gaussian, exponential, exponential-power, or fixed kernel | Gaussian or exponential, including mixtures with means | Gaussian or exponential, alone or with means |
| Weighted SA, skewness, or kurtosis | Gaussian, exponential, or exponential-power | Not implemented | Not implemented |
| Estimated hard-radius surface or landscape metric | Supported, including mixtures with exponential-power means | Not implemented for the discontinuous radius | Not implemented |
| Fixed-radius metric | Prepared once and used as a native predictor | Ordinary numeric predictor with verified original preparation | Ordinary numeric predictor with verified original preparation |

The analytic rows include `profile_glm`, `joint_nb2`, `conditional_logit`, and
`joint_mixed`, subject to their response and formula restrictions.
`profile_glm`, `joint_nb2` and `conditional_logit` accept native R product,
crossing and nesting terms involving numeric kernel predictors, including
factor interactions. Native terms and fitted contrasts define the columns.
Kernel-only scalar arithmetic and supported smooth base functions retain their
native coefficient basis. Learned dynamic bases, fixed context within a dynamic
expression, arbitrary or nondifferentiable functions, and kernel offsets remain
guarded.
Bayesian preparation, targets, prediction, conditional coefficient proposals,
and covariate curves use the same native response products with frozen contrast
and fixed-transformation metadata. Private marginal/factorized components retain
their structural and numerical admission requirements. Joint mixed models use native response products and factor coding for their
supported count families, with independent cold/native/Hessian audits. Their
raw fixed-transform inputs are retained for effect curves; scale uncertainty
remains unavailable. GAMs use native refitting, preserving their smooth
and penalty targets.
Exponential-power means are supported by the profile GLM/NB2 machinery;
the conditional-logistic, joint mixed, and Bayesian adapters require Gaussian or exponential
kernels. Analytic and Bayesian kernel means require distance bins. Weighted SQ
also needs retained raw cells, matching source definitions, and explicit row IDs.

A fixed-radius metric has no estimated bandwidth. Keep its original prepared
numeric column in the native model frame or Bayesian `data`. Analytic and
Bayesian fits use it like any other numeric covariate, including in a Bayesian
scale formula. It retains the mean and sample SD from the original preparation;
the prior-median reference for optimized spatial predictors does not replace
that normalization. Undefined and constant metrics remain preparation errors.

For new points, provide fixed columns explicitly or use `include_fixed = TRUE`
with matching spatial inputs. Automatic preparation verifies the original
source, metric, radius, kernel, resolution, buffer extent (`max_D`), and row identities.
Use the original buffer extent even when the fixed radius itself is smaller;
a shorter buffer can omit cells needed by the metric. It does not learn
a new center or SD from the prediction batch. Bayesian prediction and simulation
share this option, including repeated observations linked by explicit site IDs.
Fixed radii do not add an AIC parameter, a bandwidth prior, or scale uncertainty.

SQ is the square root of the weighted centered variance, with the sum of
weights in the denominator. Constant support has SQ zero. Standardized higher
moments are undefined at zero spread. Weighting removes discrete changes in
neighborhood membership, but does not make every metric differentiable at every
parameter value. The derivative-based methods therefore retain explicit
feature restrictions.

For native exponential-power mixtures, a hard-radius predictor has no shape
parameter. Its reported shape and shape SE are `NA`, and model selection
excludes the ignored shape position. The starting parameter vector keeps its
existing full layout. A fixed-radius metric has neither an estimated radius nor
an estimated shape. If all features are fixed, fit the native regression
directly to the prepared columns rather than asking for scale optimization.

## Prepare means, weighted SQ, and a fixed metric together

These two small surfaces share a projected square grid. Multiple covariates
can come from the same source raster; their aliases identify the model columns.

```{r artificial-surfaces}
hab <- terra::rast(nrows = 24, ncols = 24, xmin = 0, xmax = 240,
                   ymin = 0, ymax = 240, crs = "EPSG:3857")
xy <- terra::xyFromCell(hab, seq_len(terra::ncell(hab)))
terra::values(hab) <- sin(xy[, 1] / 17) + cos(xy[, 2] / 23) + xy[, 1] / 150
names(hab) <- "habitat"
elev <- hab
terra::values(elev) <- 30 + xy[, 1] / 8 + sin(xy[, 2] / 11) *
  (1 + xy[, 1] / 30) + cos(xy[, 1] / 13 + xy[, 2] / 19)
names(elev) <- "elevation"
landscape <- c(hab, elev)
locations <- expand.grid(x = seq(45, 195, 30), y = seq(45, 195, 30))
points <- terra::vect(as.matrix(locations), crs = terra::crs(hab))

features <- msr_vars(
  mean = kernel_var("habitat"),
  rough = surface_var("elevation", "sq", weighted = TRUE),
  fixed = surface_var("elevation", "sa", radius = 25)
)
prepared <- kernel_prep(points, landscape, max_D = 40,
  sigma = c(19, 29), scale_vars = features, bin = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
head(prepared$kernel_dat)
```

**How to read the output.** `mean` and `rough` are different variables with
starting bandwidths of 19 and 29 map units. `fixed` uses a radius of 25.
Preparation centers each column and divides by its sample SD. It does not
estimate a regression or select a scale. Keep the prepared row names when
joining responses and nonspatial predictors.

A native refit can use all three columns. Here `season` is a nonspatial factor,
and the counts are deterministic artificial values used only to illustrate the
calls. Heavy fitting remains explicit:

```{r native-starting-model}
dat <- prepared$kernel_dat
dat$season <- factor(rep(c("spring", "fall"), length.out = nrow(dat)))
dat$y <- (seq_len(nrow(dat)) %% 5L) + as.integer(dat$rough > 0)
model <- glm(y ~ mean + rough + fixed + season, data = dat, family = poisson())
```

```{r fit-refit, eval=FALSE}
fit <- multiScale_optim(model, prepared, backend = "refit", verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit)
profile <- profile_sigma(fit, n_pts = 10)
plot(profile)
```

**How to read these outputs.** `scale_est` reports the selected bandwidths in
map units. The fixed metric contributes a regression coefficient but no fitted
scale. Check convergence, search-bound, precision, and likelihood-profile
diagnostics before interpreting the selected values. A finite estimate or a
drawn curve does not establish identification. Hard-radius profiles can be
stepped and have no smooth-curvature scale SE.

For year-specific maps, use `kernel_prep_by_group()` and retain the map
assignment for every row. Optimization uses pooled training normalization.
Bayesian fits instead retain their declared pooled prior-reference
normalization for every draw. Neither workflow standardizes each projected
year separately. See `vignette("year-specific-rasters", package = "multiScaleR")`.

## Compare smoothing engines and prepare a map

Both FFT and direct focal calculation support the declared mean, surface, and
landscape metric families. The following calls use the same prepared circular
footprint. They perform no fitting:

```{r compare-smoothing}
map_fft <- kernel_scale.raster(landscape, multiScaleR = prepared,
  match_buffer = TRUE, fft = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
map_focal <- kernel_scale.raster(landscape, multiScaleR = prepared,
  match_buffer = TRUE, fft = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
max(abs(terra::values(map_fft) - terra::values(map_focal)), na.rm = TRUE)
terra::plot(map_fft[["rough"]], main = "Weighted SQ in source elevation units")
```

**How to read the output and map.** The printed maximum is the numerical
difference between engines. SQ describes local variation in elevation, not
mean elevation. The map retains the source units because this call did not
request standardization. Available finite cells are renormalized at edges, and
central source `NA` cells remain masked. With `na.rm = FALSE`, incomplete
footprints return `NA`; `match_buffer = TRUE` requires `na.rm = TRUE`.

The default `pct_wt` window remains available. For fitted raster prediction,
`match_buffer = TRUE` matches the retained preparation footprint, including
partially intersecting cells with their ordinary full-cell weights. Binning,
rasterization, incomplete source coverage, and the difference between an
arbitrary sample point and a cell center remain separate approximations.

## Predict points, scenarios, and rasters

For new points, prepare matching source definitions, then supply both their
data rows and spatial inputs. Selected scales and training normalization are
reused. Explicit `join_by` keys support repeated scenarios at the same site.
Verified fixed-radius normalization is opt-in:

```{r point-and-map-prediction, eval=FALSE}
# These rows and buffers illustrate the interface at the original locations.
point_prediction <- predict(fit, dat, prepared, include_fixed = TRUE,
  se.fit = TRUE, uncertainty = "conditional")
snapshot <- prepare_prediction(fit, dat, prepared, include_fixed = TRUE)
predict(snapshot)

# Factors need explicit fitted levels. Numeric site variables use their
# native units, and offset_values contains raw inputs to offset expressions.
map_inputs <- kernel_scale.raster(landscape, multiScaleR = fit,
  scale_center = TRUE, include_fixed = TRUE, match_buffer = TRUE,
  site_values = list(season = "spring"), verbose = FALSE)
response_map <- predict(fit, map_inputs, se.fit = TRUE,
  uncertainty = "conditional", raster_args = list(cores = 1))
terra::plot(response_map)
```

**How to read the predictions.** Point estimates and maps describe the
provider's expected response or selected native component. An SE map conditions
on the selected spatial scales and excludes observation noise. Analytic
GLM/NB2 maps use the same retained coefficient information as point predictions.
Other native providers supply their own conditional SEs, when available.
An unavailable native SE raises an error rather than becoming zero.

Categorical scenarios retain fitted levels. Checked raster prediction restores
logical columns to their fitted type and preserves a `projection_contract`
with the preparation controls. Supply compound offset inputs explicitly, for
example `offset_values = c(effort = 2, duration = 4)` for
`offset(log(effort * duration))`. A log offset defaults to raw value one, while
a direct offset defaults to zero. Unknown scenario names are errors.

Random-effect controls keep their native meaning. For glmmTMB or lme4,
`native_args = list(re.form = NA)` sets response random effects to zero.
For nlme, use `native_args = list(level = 0)`. These are reference predictions,
not averages over a random-effect distribution. Cox maps describe linear
predictors or relative risks. Conditional-logistic response probabilities
require complete point choice sets; a raster can instead show link or relative
risk scores. Unmarked components such as state or detection must be selected
explicitly for raster prediction and retain their native row-layout rules.

A snapshot binds fixed rows, controls, and numerical results. Prepare it again
after changing any of them. Raster preparation descriptors check retained
definitions and scaling; they do not verify the scientific provenance of map
contents. Recompute after editing layers or using file formats that discard R
attributes.

## Plot effects and compare models with the appropriate target

```{r effects-and-selection, eval=FALSE}
plot_marginal_effects(fit)
null_model <- glm(y ~ 1, data = dat, family = poisson())
aic_tab(list(spatial = fit, null = null_model), AICc = FALSE)
bic_tab(list(spatial = fit, null = null_model))
```

**How to read the plots and tables.** Numeric effect panels vary one predictor
while holding the others at their means. Factor panels use observed levels.
Frequentist bands condition on selected spatial scales. Mixed-model panels use
native response means at zero random effects, including the fitted
zero-inflation or truncated-family mean where applicable. AIC/BIC counts include
estimated scales and applicable shapes, alongside the native likelihood
parameters. Fixed radii and inapplicable hard-radius shapes do not add to K.

Comparison requires the same used observations and comparable likelihoods.
Recoverable responses, row IDs, weights, binomial trials, likelihood measures,
ML/REML settings, and Cox strata are checked. Missing native metadata still
requires user judgment. REML comparisons require a common fixed-effect design.
Bayesian fits are rejected by `aic_tab()` and `bic_tab()` because their posterior
target includes priors. Posterior predictive comparison needs a separate
workflow with its own target and diagnostics.

For Bayesian fits, `plot_marginal_effects(bayes_fit)` uses stored
response-coefficient draws at hypothetical predictor values under the fixed reference
normalization. Its bands are central credible intervals. It sets response
random effects to zero and does not reevaluate the landscape at every kernel
draw. For location-specific posterior expectations, use
`predict(bayes_fit, ..., kernel_inputs = new_preparation)`; use `simulate()`
when observation variation is needed. A selected-scale raster cannot replace
posterior integration over scales. Private unpenalized marginal-likelihood SQ
limiting routines remain gated pending their separate rank and boundary audits.

| Output | Spatial scales | Included uncertainty |
|:-------|:---------------|:---------------------|
| Native-refit point or raster SE | Selected values held fixed | Native coefficient uncertainty, where available |
| Analytic GLM/NB2 joint point interval | Estimated scales and shapes | Joint coefficient/kernel information, if all gates pass |
| Bayesian spatial expectation | Recomputed for retained joint draws | Posterior uncertainty under the declared group policies |
| Bayesian effect panel | Fixed hypothetical reference-normalized covariates | Stored marginal coefficient draws |
| Bayesian observation simulation | Recomputed for retained joint draws | Posterior uncertainty plus observation variation |

## Quick reference

```{r full-workflow, eval=FALSE}
# 1. Declare features and preserve point IDs during preparation and joins.
prepared <- kernel_prep(points, landscape, max_D = 40,
  scale_vars = features, sigma = c(19, 29), bin = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
dat <- data.frame(y = dat$y, season = dat$season, prepared$kernel_dat)

# 2. Fit an appropriate likelihood and inspect its original diagnostics.
model <- glm(y ~ mean + rough + fixed + season, dat, family = poisson())
fit <- multiScale_optim(model, prepared, backend = "refit", verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit)

# 3. Reuse training normalization for points and an explicit map scenario.
predict(fit, dat, prepared, include_fixed = TRUE)
map_inputs <- kernel_scale.raster(landscape, multiScaleR = fit,
  scale_center = TRUE, include_fixed = TRUE, match_buffer = TRUE,
  site_values = list(season = "spring"), verbose = FALSE)
response_map <- predict(fit, map_inputs)

# 4. Read effects as conditional curves and compare sampling likelihoods.
plot_marginal_effects(fit)
aic_tab(list(fit, glm(y ~ 1, dat, family = poisson())), AICc = FALSE)
```

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `msr_vars()` | Name source-specific means and metrics |
| `kernel_prep()` / `kernel_prep_by_group()` | Prepare matching spatial rows and retain normalization |
| `multiScale_optim()` / `multiScale_bayes()` | Fit a supported likelihood or posterior target |
| `kernel_scale.raster()` | Evaluate the same declared features on a raster grid |
| `predict()` / `prepare_prediction()` | Predict with explicit spatial and uncertainty contracts |
| `plot_marginal_effects()` | Display conditional or hypothetical reference-covariate effects |
| `aic_tab()` / `bic_tab()` | Compare appropriate sampling likelihoods |

See also:

- `vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` for the core fitting workflow.
- `vignette("surface_metric_covariates", package = "multiScaleR")` for texture definitions and interpretation.
- `vignette("landscape_metric_covariates", package = "multiScaleR")` for categorical metrics.
- `vignette("inference-contracts", package = "multiScaleR")` for likelihood, posterior, and uncertainty distinctions.
- `vignette("bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR")` for joint-draw spatial expectations and observation simulation.

One-kernel NB2 `scale_inference()` assessments retain native products and factor
contrasts in constrained, unrestricted, and bootstrap refits. The zero-effect
diagnostic removes every response column involving that kernel. It is a
feasible likelihood ceiling, not a calibrated test for an interaction or kernel
effect. Existing kernel-mean coverage studies do not establish interval coverage
for weighted SQ or interactions. All starts, failures, cold checks, dispersion
boundaries, and uncertainty qualifications remain part of the assessment.

### Relative step-selection projections

For `conditional_logit`, `type = "link"` returns the uncentered linear selection
index, and the exact type `"risk"` returns its exponential. These scores need
matching spatial inputs and the fixed formula variables, but no prediction
choice-set IDs. They describe relative selection, not occurrence probabilities
or a utilization distribution. Standard errors require
`uncertainty = "conditional"` and hold the estimated kernel parameters fixed.

`type = "response"` still normalizes within complete caller-defined choice sets,
with at least two alternatives in each set. A snapshot without valid set IDs
supports link and risk outputs, records why response probabilities are
unavailable, and refuses a response request. It does not invent groups.

Checked analytic raster prediction retains every native coefficient column,
including kernel-by-factor products and fixed learned transformations. Raster
standard errors remain conditional on the selected scales. The normalization
engine uses one registered native call with stable max shifting; independent
native likelihood and cold-start checks remain in place. No comparative speedup
is claimed from validation performed alongside other R work.

Conditional-backend link and risk scores leave formula offsets unshifted. Risk
standard errors use the delta method, `risk * SE(link)`, conditional on the
selected kernel. Native survival predictions retain their provider's reference
and standard-error conventions; do not equate them merely because both outputs
are called risk.

### Formula expansion and kernel arithmetic

R treats `habitat * year` as main effects plus their interaction. `habitat:year`
requests the interaction alone. Formula powers expand crossings; `habitat^2`
is not a numeric square. Use `I(habitat^2)` for a quadratic response term.

Kernel-only scalar expressions support arithmetic and the base functions `exp`,
`log`, `sqrt`, `sin`, `cos`, and `tan`. They act on the standardized kernel
predictors after extraction. They do not transform raster cells before
smoothing. Native coefficient columns, contrasts, normalized priors and the
original fixed reference transformation are retained. Priors remain expressed
in that chosen native coefficient basis.

Expressions must be pointwise functions of optimized kernels and literal
constants. Fixed-data inputs inside a dynamic expression, learned dynamic
bases, arbitrary or nondifferentiable functions, and kernel-valued offsets
retain explicit guards. Nonfinite domains are errors, with no clipping.
All fitting, covariance, native refit, scale-profile and private-admission
safeguards still apply. Supporting a formula does not establish identification
or calibrated intervals.


For unmarked effect curves, active native terms select the panels. Removing a
term removes its panel; offsets still supply prediction inputs, and random-only
grouping columns do not receive panels. Admitted quoted names, such as
`` `land:cover` ``, and fixed expressions retain their native coefficient basis
and conditional intervals.

A pipe inside `I(a | b)` is a fixed logical operation in R. The native unmarked
parser can nevertheless reject that expression, or a quoted name containing a
pipe, before fitting. Precompute the logical predictor as a named column and
rename pipe-containing columns before the native fit when this happens. For complete,
nonmissing logical inputs, `I(as.integer(a) + as.integer(b) > 0)` also expresses
a fixed OR without a pipe token. With missing inputs, precompute the original
`a | b` expression to retain R's missing-value logic. These preparations are explicit; multiScaleR does not
silently replace a native random-effect declaration or alter the fitted target.


For supported ordinary unmarked occupancy and count curves, a learned fixed
basis such as `poly(temperature, 2)` or `scale(temperature)` retains its training
prediction call, including the equivalent `stats::poly()` and `base::scale()`
forms. The plotting grid does not recenter, rescale, or refit that
basis. Curves use native coefficient covariance and inverse links, with random
effects set to zero; they remain conditional on the fitted spatial scales.


Known qualified fixed transformations use the evaluated training metadata in
profile GLM/NB2 and prepared response/scale formulas. Subset and new prediction
rows retain the original center and spread for `base::scale()`. Fixed logical
expressions inside `I()` retain R meaning during preparation; formula random
terms remain subject to the existing additive-intercept contract.

The supported one-case conditional-logistic adapter preserves original fixed
training metadata when removing the choice-set stratum. Qualified fixed
`base::scale()` and `stats::poly()` calls keep their original expression names,
contrasts, offsets, and coefficient geometry. This does not admit additional Cox
structures or provide joint scale uncertainty.

Fixed training transformations also apply to new rows with a constant predictor,
reordered sites, saved prediction snapshots, and raster prediction blocks.
Qualified `base::scale()` calls use the original training center and spread.
Native fixed spline terms retain their training knots and boundaries. These
checks preserve coefficient-conditional uncertainty; they do not establish
joint scale uncertainty or admit additional model structures.


Native LM/GLM, GAM, lme4, glmmTMB and time-fixed, unpenalized Cox prediction routes retain
fixed training transformations for qualified `base::scale()` and `stats::poly()`
calls. This applies to point predictions, prepared numerical snapshots, raster
blocks and effect curves when the original raw curve variables are available.
A single new value or a constant raster does not define a new standard deviation.
The native coefficients, covariance, fitted likelihood and diagnostics stay fixed.

Full analytic fits saved before this repair can recover prediction metadata
from their retained evaluated native frame. Numerical-only snapshots have no
such frame, so prepare them again from the full fit. This recovery does not
supply missing raw variables for a curve, change a prior, add joint scale
uncertainty or qualify a new model component. Unsupported native GAM layouts
that require a metadata change remain explicitly guarded pending component tests.

## GAMs with multiple linear predictors

Native refit predictions retain the complete component structure of a fitted
`mgcv::gam()` model. Each component uses its fitted fixed transformations,
factor contrasts and coefficient columns. Point predictions, numerical
snapshots and checked rasters retain native link, response, term and basis
outputs. Select term outputs with the native `terms` or `exclude` controls.
The native warning for unavailable multi-predictor `iterms` behavior is retained.

Response columns depend on the family. A Gaussian location-scale (`gaulss`)
fit returns its mean and reciprocal standard deviation. A multinomial fit
returns category probabilities, which can outnumber its linear predictors.
Here the family's scale describes response variation. The ecological kernel
bandwidths remain separate fitted spatial parameters.
These columns are not interchangeable and the prediction contract records the
native family and number of linear predictors.

Native standard errors require `uncertainty = "conditional"`. The
`unconditional = TRUE` native control requests mgcv's smoothing-parameter
covariance correction when available. Both choices condition on the selected
ecological kernel scales. Neither is a full Bayesian ecological-scale
prediction. Snapshot preparation stores numerical outputs and the selected
controls, rather than a fitted model or its formula environment.

For effect curves, select a native output column with `component`. The default
`link = FALSE` plots a linear predictor. Set `link = TRUE` to plot a native
response column. For multinomial fits the number of response columns can exceed
the number of linear predictors. These curves use native output-scale Wald
limits and hold the fitted kernel scales and smoothing parameters fixed.
Fixed metadata recovery does not recover discarded raw fitting data or qualify
data-dependent transformations inside smooth terms.

## Supply raw reference rows for transformed effect curves

A fitted model frame may retain `poly(temperature, 2)`, `I(elevation^2)` or a
compound offset without retaining the corresponding raw columns. A square
cannot establish the sign of its original input. An orthogonal polynomial
basis also needs its fitted prediction metadata. Supply `reference_data` when
you retained the raw predictor values separately. This option is available for
checked native LM/GLM, GAM and time-fixed, unpenalized Cox structures.

Reference rows need explicit row names identifying the retained fitted rows.
The function matches those IDs, evaluates the fitted prediction terms and
checks every retained feature, native design or smooth basis, factor coding
and formula offset. Nonfinite values, missing rows or inputs, new levels and
changed features raise an error. The comparison uses the fitted transformation
and contrasts. It does not relearn them on the supplied rows or on a plotting
grid.

```{r raw-reference-curves, eval=FALSE}
# training_data contains the raw predictors for these actual fitted rows.
fit_rows <- row.names(fit$opt_mod$model)
index <- match(fit_rows, row.names(training_data))
stopifnot(!anyNA(index))
reference <- training_data[index, , drop = FALSE]
row.names(reference) <- fit_rows

# Supply the matched raw context, including raw inputs to formula offsets.
curves <- plot_marginal_effects(fit, reference_data = reference)
attr(curves, "reference_data_contract")

# For a multiple-predictor GAM, select the output column explicitly.
link_curves <- plot_marginal_effects(gam_fit, reference_data = gam_reference,
  component = 2)
response_curves <- plot_marginal_effects(gam_fit, reference_data = gam_reference,
  component = 2, link = TRUE)
```

For native refits, the reference must contain the final fitted, standardized
spatial columns alongside the raw fixed predictors. Retain those columns
during fitting. Analytic GLM/NB2 and admitted conditional-logistic fits rebuild
selected kernel values from their verified preparation before checking the
reference. Original preparation and normalization remain authoritative.

Passing this check establishes observable feature equivalence for the claimed
row IDs. It cannot prove a unique original raw value from a many-to-one
transformation. The returned `reference_data_contract` records that limitation.
The model is not refit and its coefficients, covariance, diagnostics and priors
remain unchanged. Curves remain conditional on the fitted ecological scales.

Unmarked and Bayesian curves retain their existing structured-data and
posterior-reference requirements. External call offsets, unsupported native
structures, matrix-valued raw curve inputs and nested learned transformations
without fixed prediction metadata remain guarded. A supplied raw data frame
does not remove those requirements.

Conditional-logistic Cox curves default to log relative risk. Their
`link = TRUE` curves exponentiate that score, including for a native `clogit`
fit. These are relative selection scores rather than occurrence probabilities
or probabilities normalized within a complete choice set.

Native GAM predictions also retain the fitted factor coding when a factor
appears only inside an interaction. Changing session contrast options after
fitting does not redefine these package predictions. Factor levels come from
the retained fitting metadata, including for single-row or blocked prediction.
Coefficients, covariance and fitting diagnostics stay unchanged. Additional
GAM providers retain their own native prediction methods.

Logical expressions such as `I(z > 0)` can appear in GAM interactions.
Prediction retains their logical type and the fitted coding, including when
a prediction block contains only `TRUE` or only `FALSE`. This also applies
to multi-component GAMs and verified raw-reference curves.

For `mgcv::ziplss()` models, `plot_marginal_effects(..., link = TRUE,
component = 1, reference_data = raw_data)` selects the overall expected count
across absence and presence. Both linear predictors contribute to that mean.
Response standard errors propagate their full coefficient covariance,
including signed cross-covariance. The original native mean is retained.
The resulting Wald limits describe uncertainty in the mean. They omit count
noise and uncertainty in the selected ecological scales, and can extend below
zero. With `link = FALSE`, the two original link predictors remain selectable.
The prediction contract identifies the covariance calculation separately from
the provider's response-SE formula. Native smoothing-covariance controls keep
their meaning for point and prepared predictions.

Ordinary native Cox and `survival::clogit()` refits can recover qualified
fixed scaling and polynomial metadata from their retained evaluated training
frames. Unequal subsets, one-row predictions, numerical snapshots, checked
raster blocks and verified raw-reference curves reuse the fitting definition.
Linear predictors and relative risk keep their native meanings and conditional
standard errors; neither is a within-step choice probability. Recovery does
not change event counts, native parameter degrees of freedom, coefficients,
covariance, likelihood or diagnostics. Missing evaluated frames and metadata
changes for penalized, time-varying or multistate structures remain guarded.

Package predictions from native `mgcv::bam()` fits retain the fitted factor
coding when session contrasts change. Native block controls and optimized
discrete prediction remain in place. Native parallel prediction workers also
receive saved coding and explicit term exclusions. Their mgcv version and
prediction implementation must match the parent; a mismatch stops prediction.
The checks use declared Gaussian software fixtures, not a speed benchmark or
an interval-calibration study. Mean standard errors keep the native coefficient
covariance target and omit ecological-scale uncertainty and observation noise.
Numerical snapshots cache the requested outputs without retaining a worker pool.


For ordinary BAM prediction, `type = "iterms"` returns a row-by-term matrix,
including its native intercept constant. Worker prediction retains that
geometry, selected or excluded terms, and the `iterms.type` control. These
routes also support native Gaussian BAM fits without factors and fits whose
formula contains only smooth terms. The optimized discrete provider resets
`iterms` to `terms` and issues its native warning. Use `discrete = FALSE` when
you need ordinary `iterms`; for a numerical snapshot, bind this choice with
`native_args = list(discrete = FALSE)` and `component = "iterms"`.

An `unconditional = TRUE` request does not guarantee an available
smoothing-adjusted covariance. Native BAM may discard that covariance and
warn that the correction is unavailable. Its coefficient-covariance decision
is preserved, and warning conditions from ordinary prediction workers also
reach the parent call. Read these SEs as conditional on the ecological scales;
they do not include observation noise or full-posterior uncertainty. Native
EDF and likelihood parameter counts remain distinct from the two selected
ecological parameters in the declared Gaussian software checks.


Native mgcv versions may also warn when selecting or excluding terms from a
model with no parametric coefficients. That provider warning is retained
alongside the native numerical result. It is separate from the fitted-mode
convergence, score and curvature checks.


Warnings transported from ordinary BAM workers retain their native messages,
classes and prediction controls. Their calls identify the native method and
refer to fitted models and prediction rows symbolically, avoiding extra copies
of those data in warning payloads. Provider version and the symbolic argument
names remain attached as diagnostic context. The worker's original warning
is retained; unrelated native warning calls are unchanged.


Native Gaussian, binomial and Poisson BAM fits use the shared point,
numerical-snapshot, checked-map and raw-reference curve routes. Ordinary
prediction supports factor interactions, `I(z^2)` terms and native smooths;
set `discrete = FALSE` when requesting ordinary `iterms` output. Native
parallel scalar and matrix outputs retain their provider geometry, which can
differ from serial geometry. Term matrices retain their labels and intercept
constant. Native likelihood degrees of freedom supply the coefficient,
smoothing and family-dispersion contribution to AIC/BIC; only selected
ecological scale parameters and applicable expow shapes are added.

For a single-predictor GAM or BAM, `plot_marginal_effects()` inherits the GLM
automatic response transformation. Both values of `link` retain response
curves, with inverse-link bounds from conditional link-scale Wald intervals.
Use `predict(..., type = "link")` for link-scale predictions. Multi-component
GAM curves have an explicit component choice: `link = FALSE` selects a linear
predictor and `link = TRUE` selects a native response component. These
conventions preserve the existing interfaces.

Binomial response predictions are probabilities, including models fitted to
success/failure counts. Trial counts enter the fitted likelihood and
covariance; they do not automatically convert predictions to counts for new
trials. Poisson response predictions are conditional expected counts. Neither
response SEs nor these curve intervals add ecological-scale uncertainty,
observation noise or full-posterior uncertainty. Native BAM rejects general
families; use an appropriate native GAM for multi-predictor families instead.
